newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: YEAREND-Malaysian interest rates seen staying firm.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Malaysian interest rates seen staying firm.

text.p: Malaysia is expected to maintain tight monetary policy for at least the first six months of 1997 as high broad money supply remains a concern for the fast-growing economy, economists said on Monday.
This meant interest rates would stay at current levels with the benchmark three-month interbank rate remaining at around 7.30 percent, they said.
On Monday, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) was at 7.36 percent.

The Singapore-based research firm I.D.E.A. said in a commentary that with loan growth still high and strong economic growth expected in the first half of 1997, there could be fresh inflationary pressures in the economy.

"There remains a likelihood that the benchmark three-month KLIBOR would remain in the 7.30/40 percent region throughout the first quarter of 1997 in order to keep inflationary pressures in check," I.D.E.A said.
Malaysia reported an inflation rate of 3.4 percent last year. It has forecast a rate of 3.6 percent in 1996 and 3.5 percent next year.
In a Reuters poll last month, 10 research houses had forecast three-month KLIBOR at an average 7.18 percent in March, 1997, and at 7.03 percent at the end of the second quarter.

Economists said the monetary figures announced by the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, in the last two months had made them alter their forecasts to steady interest rates in the medium-term, from an earlier prediction of a decline in rates.
Bank Negara on Friday announced that broad money supply, known as M3, grew by 21.7 percent year-on-year in November against 22.6 percent in October.
"M3 should be kept below 20 percent for a moderate period of time, say six to nine months, which we have not seen yet," said an economist with a Singapore-based research house.
In addition, recent comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that hinted at possible interest rate increases in the U.S. would put pressure on Malaysia, he said.
"The rates will hold (at the current level), at least in the first half of next year," the head of money dealing at a Malaysian bank said.
He said there could be a slight easing in the second half of 1997 if the mildly contractionary fiscal policy announced in the annual budget eases the burden on monetary policy.
"If growth slows down remarkably next year, then we may see the central bank lowering rates, conservatively, from the second quarter (of 1997) onwards," said the head of a Malaysian research firm.

Malaysia's growing current account deficit had triggered worries about overheating last year and forced it to maintain tight monetary policy. The three-month interbank rate has risen by nearly 200 basis points in the last two years.
Some dealers said the sharp improvement on the trade balance front could favour an interest rate drop.
Malaysia has recorded a lower trade deficit of 954.35 million ringgit ($378.7 million) in the first 10 months of 1996 against around 9.96 billion in the same period last year.

Malaysia expects gross domestic product growth to slow down to 8.0 percent a year until 2000 from 9.5 percent in 1995. It has forecast growth at 8.2 percent for 1996, making it the ninth successive year of more than eight percent growth.
($1=2.52 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
